newsitem.title: USA: Argentine peso debt rating may lift domestic bonds.
newsitem.headline: Argentine peso debt rating may lift domestic bonds.

text.p: Argentina's first peso-denominated sovereign debt rating could speed the contraction of the spread between dollar and peso debt, which may give Argentine corporations greater flexibility in the capital markets, U.S. analysts said.
Moody's Investors Service assigned on Tuesday a B1 rating to peso-denominated long-term sovereign debt issued by Argentina, the same rating for its foreign currency debt.
"Investors will find local currency debt undervalued," said an analyst with a major U.S. investment house.
The peso debt has been trading below the dollar debt because of an assumed premium for convertibility risk and the identical rating could eliminate some of the differentials, he said.

Argentina adopted a currency board system that pegs the peso to the dollar in 1992 and the parity "intrinsically equates the credit risk in local currency debt to that of foreign currency obligations," according to Moody's release.
Normally, a country's local currency debt is rated higher than its foreign currency debt, said another analyst who preferred not to be named.
She cited the examples of Mexico and South Africa, whose local currency debts are rated two notches higher than their foreign currency counterparts.
The same B1 rating for both local and foreign currency debts acknowledges the constraint imposed by the currency board system on paying its domestic debt, she said.
"Argentina does not have the flexibility of printing money to meet its peso obligations," the analyst said.
Previously, in times of political uncertainty, investors lost confidence in peso debt faster than in foreign currency debt, said a trader.

The trader said the spread of the peso over the dollar widened dramatically when Domingo Cavallo resigned. He forecast the peso debt would always maintain a premium over the dollar debt even as the currency board appeared solid.
Cavallo, Argentine Economy minister and widely credited as the father of the convertibility plan, resigned in July 1996.
Omar Borla, chief Latin America economist at Robert Flemings Inc, said that, since the currency board was put in place, foreign investment in both the peso and the dollar sovereign papers soared.

Regardless of their political stripes, Argentine policy makers are fully committed to the currency board, recognizing that the abandonment of parity means devaluation and an end to the foreign investment boom, he said.
This year, the Argentine government plans to raise $4 billion to $4.5 billion dollars' worth of debt internally, a huge sum for the domestic market, Borla said.

The spread between the dollar prime rates and the peso prime rates charged by Argentine banks averaged about 200 basis points for the year in 1996, but by the end of the year the differential declined to about 160 basis points, he said.
Currently, it is less costly for Argentine corporations to borrow in dollars, but as the spread shrinks further they would have more flexibility to tap in either markets, he said.
